evidence.claim: The authorities reacted quickly and decisively to the pandemic by announcing support packages worth Tk 1.9 trillion, financed partly by curtailing non-priority current spending and suspending low-priority capital projects.
evidence.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2021 Article IV Consultation with Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The authorities reacted quickly and decisively to the pandemic by announcing support packages worth Tk 1.9 trillion, financed partly by curtailing non-priority current spending and suspending low-priority capital projects.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct IMF statement summarizing a concrete fiscal response and its financing logic.
evidence.period_fit: Immediate policy baseline for the 2022 year, though describing the pandemic response that carried into 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Bangladesh authorities during the Hasina government.
contrary_evidence: The IMF also notes that higher inflation and wider fiscal deficits remained a downside risk.

evidence.claim: IMF directors commended fiscal prudence and low debt distress, but urged revenue administration and tax reform, stronger banking regulation and corporate governance, and action to stem non-performing loans in state-owned banks.
evidence.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2021 Article IV Consultation with Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: IMF directors commended fiscal prudence and low debt distress, but urged revenue administration and tax reform, stronger banking regulation and corporate governance, and action to stem non-performing loans in state-owned banks.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IMF executive-board assessment with explicit policy priorities and critique.
evidence.period_fit: Covers the policy baseline relevant to 2022 and identifies active weaknesses during the year.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government and its economic institutions, not a personal action by Hasina alone.
contrary_evidence: The same assessment acknowledges strong economic growth and social development, so the picture is mixed rather than uniformly negative.

evidence.claim: Social safety-net spending was budgeted at 3.2 percent of GDP in FY22; expanded programs included widow and old-age allowances, a new urban-poor database, and cash transfers totaling Tk 27 billion for about 9 million people, with G2P and mobile-finance tools used to improve transparency and reach.
evidence.title: Bangladesh: 2021 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: Social safety-net spending was budgeted at 3.2 percent of GDP in FY22; expanded programs included widow and old-age allowances, a new urban-poor database, and cash transfers totaling Tk 27 billion for about 9 million people, with G2P and mobile-finance tools used to improve transparency and reach.
evidence.source_locator: Annex V / social safety net section in the search-result excerpt
evidence.source_confidence_reason: IMF staff report excerpt is highly relevant, though the full page was not directly fetchable in this environment.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers FY22 and the 2022 policy environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Bangladesh authorities under Hasina; the implementation channel was the finance and social protection apparatus.
contrary_evidence: The excerpt also says health and education spending remained low, so the social-protection gains did not erase broader financing gaps.

evidence.claim: The IMF and Bangladesh authorities reached a 42-month ECF/EFF and RSF agreement aimed at preserving macroeconomic stability, supporting strong inclusive and green growth, and protecting the vulnerable.
evidence.title: IMF Staff Reaches Staff-Level Agreement with Bangladesh on the Extended Credit Facility/Extended Fund Facility and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility
evidence.excerpt: The IMF and Bangladesh authorities reached a 42-month ECF/EFF and RSF agreement aimed at preserving macroeconomic stability, supporting strong inclusive and green growth, and protecting the vulnerable.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IMF statement on a major 2022 policy arrangement with explicit goals and country attribution.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers late 2022 and the 2022 shock environment.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Bangladesh authorities under the Hasina government.
contrary_evidence: The agreement itself implies prior macro strain, not a clean success story.

evidence.claim: Key elements of the program included higher revenue mobilization, spending rationalization, modernizing the monetary policy framework, and increasing exchange-rate flexibility.
evidence.title: IMF Staff Reaches Staff-Level Agreement with Bangladesh on the Extended Credit Facility/Extended Fund Facility and the Resilience and Sustainability Facility
evidence.excerpt: Key elements of the program included higher revenue mobilization, spending rationalization, modernizing the monetary policy framework, and increasing exchange-rate flexibility.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary IMF summary of the program's policy package, directly tied to 2022 decision-making.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Bangladesh authorities; implementation depended on the Hasina government and the central bank.
contrary_evidence: The need for a Fund program indicates that existing policy settings had not been sufficient on their own.

evidence.claim: The program supported National Tariff Policy modernization, digital technologies, e-GP procurement, and faster social-protection delivery through G2P cash transfers with gender-disaggregated data.
evidence.title: World Bank Helps Bangladesh Build Economic Resilience
evidence.excerpt: The program supported National Tariff Policy modernization, digital technologies, e-GP procurement, and faster social-protection delivery through G2P cash transfers with gender-disaggregated data.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank release with concrete policy mechanisms and implementation channels.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers 2022 policy design and implementation.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government and line ministries that implemented the program.
contrary_evidence: The press release does not prove full implementation or distributional success on its own.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Bangladesh needed a strong reform agenda to sustain growth, with key barriers in trade competitiveness, financial-sector vulnerabilities, and orderly urbanization.
evidence.title: Strong Trade Competitiveness, Financial Sector, and Well-functioning Cities are Critical for Sustained Growth in Bangladesh: World Bank
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Bangladesh needed a strong reform agenda to sustain growth, with key barriers in trade competitiveness, financial-sector vulnerabilities, and orderly urbanization.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank assessment of Bangladesh's 2022 growth constraints.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level policy environment under the Hasina government.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes Bangladesh had been among the top 10 fastest-growing economies over the prior decade.

evidence.claim: High tariffs, trade costs, weak bank asset quality, and the need for more finance for women, MSMEs, and FDI were identified as key obstacles to long-term growth and inclusion.
evidence.title: Strong Trade Competitiveness, Financial Sector, and Well-functioning Cities are Critical for Sustained Growth in Bangladesh: World Bank
evidence.excerpt: High tariffs, trade costs, weak bank asset quality, and the need for more finance for women, MSMEs, and FDI were identified as key obstacles to long-term growth and inclusion.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank text with concrete economic mechanisms and target groups.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Bangladesh's policy environment under Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The same report notes rapid digital-payment adoption and a large formal economy in Dhaka, so the system was not uniformly closed to market development.

evidence.claim: Bangladesh raised fuel prices by about 50 percent, inflation was already above 7 percent, and foreign-exchange reserves had fallen to $39.67 billion from $45.89 billion a year earlier.
evidence.title: Bangladesh announces fuel price jump, stokes inflation fears
evidence.excerpt: Bangladesh raised fuel prices by about 50 percent, inflation was already above 7 percent, and foreign-exchange reserves had fallen to $39.67 billion from $45.89 billion a year earlier.
evidence.source_locator: Reuters copy lines 428-452 in the Investing.com republication
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting with specific price, inflation, and reserve figures; republication preserves the original wire content.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Bangladesh government and energy ministry under Hasina.
contrary_evidence: Officials said the hike was unavoidable because of global market conditions, so the action was partly reactive rather than purely discretionary.

evidence.claim: The budget kept social safety net allocation at Tk113,576 crore, or 16.75 percent of the budget and 2.55 percent of GDP; the finance minister said the scope was being expanded to reduce poverty and inequality, with 29 percent of households already covered and allocations up almost eight-fold since FY08-09.
evidence.title: Budget FY23: No rise in social safety net allocation despite rise in inflation
evidence.excerpt: The budget kept social safety net allocation at Tk113,576 crore, or 16.75 percent of the budget and 2.55 percent of GDP; the finance minister said the scope was being expanded to reduce poverty and inequality, with 29 percent of households already covered and allocations up almost eight-fold since FY08-09.
evidence.source_locator: Article body and quoted finance-minister remarks
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Local reporting with specific figures and direct quotation from the budget speech.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers the FY23 budget announced in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government through the finance minister and budget framework.
contrary_evidence: The article also notes that the allocation fell proportionately versus the previous year once budget size is considered.

evidence.claim: The government appointed finance secretary Abdur Rouf Talukder as Bangladesh Bank governor; the article says he had held senior finance posts and specialized in public finance, budget reform, macroeconomic management, and IT in public financial management.
evidence.title: Bangladesh appoints Abdur Rouf Talukder as central bank governor
evidence.excerpt: The government appointed finance secretary Abdur Rouf Talukder as Bangladesh Bank governor; the article says he had held senior finance posts and specialized in public finance, budget reform, macroeconomic management, and IT in public financial management.
evidence.source_locator: Article body describing the appointment and career background
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous local reporting on a specific economic appointment with clear career details.
evidence.period_fit: Directly covers a 2022 appointment affecting monetary management.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the Hasina government; the appointment was made through the finance ministry/government notification.
contrary_evidence: The appointee was a senior civil servant rather than an independent outside technocrat, so the appointment does not prove maximal autonomy.

evidence.claim: Inflation rose to 9.5 percent in August 2022, the FY22 balance-of-payments deficit reached $5.3 billion, foreign-exchange reserves came under pressure, a multiple exchange-rate regime was introduced in September 2022, and financial-sector vulnerabilities deepened.
evidence.title: Sustaining Growth in Bangladesh with Strong Reforms
evidence.excerpt: Inflation rose to 9.5 percent in August 2022, the FY22 balance-of-payments deficit reached $5.3 billion, foreign-exchange reserves came under pressure, a multiple exchange-rate regime was introduced in September 2022, and financial-sector vulnerabilities deepened.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank assessment with concrete 2022 macro indicators and policy changes.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on 2022 with direct 2022 indicators and policy changes.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to Bangladesh's macroeconomic policy environment under Hasina.
contrary_evidence: The same piece notes Bangladesh still remained at low risk of debt distress, so the picture was stressed but not collapsed.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said extreme poverty had fallen to 5 percent in 2022, showing strong long-run poverty reduction even as sustaining growth would require policy adjustments to deal with the balance-of-payments deficit, inflation, and financial-sector vulnerabilities.
evidence.title: Structural Reforms are Essential to Sustain Growth & Poverty Reduction in Bangladesh
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said extreme poverty had fallen to 5 percent in 2022, showing strong long-run poverty reduction even as sustaining growth would require policy adjustments to deal with the balance-of-payments deficit, inflation, and financial-sector vulnerabilities.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary World Bank feature using 2022 household-survey-based data in a 2023 publication.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level outcome under the Hasina government; not a direct claim about her personal decision-making.
contrary_evidence: The same story says growth would need policy adjustments, so the poverty improvement did not eliminate macro and distributional weaknesses.

unresolved_gaps: No direct Hasina-specific 2022 decision on nuclear safety appointments, command-and-control, or emergency doctrine.
No independent audit of Rooppur safety performance or BAERA independence in the target year.
No direct Bangladesh-initiated interstate war, proxy war, or coercive military campaign in 2022.
Direct command-chain evidence for specific 2022 abuses remains thin.
Stronger direct evidence is still needed on institutional restraint, especially courts, election administration, and oversight bodies.
Household-level distribution and independent execution evidence are thinner than macro and program-announcement evidence.
Direct ruler causation for service delivery is thinner than outcome evidence.
Direct first-person evidence of correction, admission, or disclosure is still thin.
The plot-allocation/self-dealing allegations need stronger independent corroboration or final adjudication.
Independent audits of implementation quality and outcome progress are still limited compared with announced-program evidence.
Direct evidence that Hasina personally monitored, corrected, or replaced ineffective implementers is sparse.
